phenomenon.name: Marid
phenomenon.subcategory: Class of jinn in Islamic tradition

description.summary: A category of powerful, rebellious jinn in Islamic theology and Arabian folklore. The Quran (37:7) speaks of stars guarding the lowest heaven against the 'rebellious devils' (shayṭānin māridin), and later Arabic literature, including the Thousand and One Nights, treats the Marid as among the strongest classes of jinn.
description.full: Marid (Arabic مَارِد, mārid, 'rebellious') is a class of powerful jinn in Islamic theology and Arabian folklore. The term derives from the Arabic root m-r-d, meaning 'recalcitrant' or 'rebellious'. The Quran in Surah As-Saffat (37:7) describes stars adorning the lowest heaven and protecting it from 'every rebellious devil' (kulli shayṭānin māridin), establishing marids as entities that attempt to eavesdrop on heavenly affairs. Later Arabic theological and lexicographical tradition (e.g. Lisan al-Arab, Hans Wehr) treats marids as a distinct category of jinn, often paired or contrasted with the ʿifrīt: in the schema reported by some Maliki Athari scholars (such as Ibn ʿAbd al-Barr), the marid is more malevolent than an ordinary shayṭān but less powerful than an ʿifrīt; other sources reverse the ordering. In the MacNaghten edition of One Thousand and One Nights (e.g. The Story of the Fisherman and the Jinni), 'marid' and 'ifrit' are used somewhat interchangeably. Western popular culture, drawing on these stories and on later occult writing, has often pictured Marids as wish-granting water-spirits bound to vessels — a partial but distorted reflection of the Arabic tradition.

etymology.origin: Arabic active participle of the root m-r-d ('to rebel, be recalcitrant'); cognate with Hebrew מָרַד (māraḏ, 'to rebel') and Aramaic forms.
etymology.meaning: 'Rebellious one'; in Islamic usage, a powerful, rebellious jinn or devil.

related_phenomena.name: ʿIfrīt
related_phenomena.description: Another powerful class of jinn, often paired or contrasted with the marid

related_phenomena.name: Ghoul
related_phenomena.description: Another category of dangerous Arabian supernatural being

related_phenomena.name: Shayṭān
related_phenomena.description: Broad category of devils to which marids and ifrits both belong in some traditions

related_phenomena.name: Jinn
related_phenomena.description: The general class of beings created from smokeless fire in Islamic theology

features.description: Like all jinn, marids are described in Islamic theology as created from a smokeless or scorching fire
Often depicted as gigantic in Arabic literature and the Thousand and One Nights
Like other jinn, marids can take on various forms — human, animal, monstrous

physical.morphology: An invisible spiritual being capable of manifesting in physical form; in literature, often pictured as an immense humanoid.

abilities.description: Considered among the most powerful classes of jinn, capable of feats beyond ordinary jinn
Ability to take on different forms
In Quranic tradition, marids attempt to ascend toward the lowest heaven and overhear angelic speech, and are warded off by shooting stars
In epics such as Sirat Sayf ibn Dhi-Yazan, marids defy human masters and even kings

patterns: Often portrayed as proud, free-willed, and resistant to control
In folktales, may be bound by a powerful magician or by King Solomon
Western popular culture often associates Marids specifically with water; this is a later, partly Western, refinement

range.description: Pan-Islamic — present wherever Islamic theology and Arabic folklore are transmitted; especially prominent in classical Arabic literature.

first_recorded.source: Quran, Surah As-Saffat 37:7 (revealed in early 7th century CE)

peak_activity_periods.description: Classical Arabic literary, theological, and lexicographical treatment of marids and other jinn (Lisan al-Arab, Tafsir tradition).
Marids feature prominently in the Thousand and One Nights story tradition.

origins.cultural_roots: Pre-Islamic Arabian belief in jinn, integrated and reframed by Quranic revelation and subsequent Islamic theology and lexicography.
origins.folklore_connections: Connects to broader Arabic and Islamic jinn tradition (ifrit, ghoul, shayṭān) and to the literary world of the Thousand and One Nights.

timeline.event: Quran (Surah As-Saffat 37:7) describes the lowest heaven adorned with stars to guard against 'rebellious devils' (shayṭānin māridin)
timeline.significance: Earliest Quranic reference and foundational text

timeline.event: The classical Arabic story-cycle Alf Layla wa-Layla (One Thousand and One Nights) develops; marids and ifrits feature in stories such as The Fisherman and the Jinni
timeline.significance: Anchors the marid in world literature
timeline.source: MacNaghten edition of the Thousand and One Nights

timeline.event: Ibn Manzur compiles Lisan al-Arab, including detailed lexical entries on marid

history.modern_era: Marids continue to be discussed in Islamic theology and tafsir, and have entered Western popular culture chiefly via translations of the Arabian Nights and via fantasy and gaming franchises that draw on the jinn hierarchy.

documentary.name: Quran, Surah As-Saffat 37:7
documentary.description: Foundational Quranic reference to 'rebellious devils' (shayṭānin māridin) warded off from the lowest heaven.
documentary.analysis: Authoritative scriptural source for the marid as a category of jinn in Islamic tradition.

paranormal.name: Real class of jinn
paranormal.description: In Islamic theology, marids are real spiritual beings, a recognised class within the broader category of jinn created from smokeless fire.

skeptical.name: Pre-Islamic spirit-categories systematised
skeptical.description: From a comparative-religion perspective, the marid is a literary and theological systematisation of pre-Islamic Arabian beliefs about powerful spirits, integrated into Quranic cosmology.
evidence_cited: Pre-Islamic Arabian poetry references to jinn

traditions: Quranic and tafsir tradition on jinn
Arabian Nights / Thousand and One Nights literary tradition
stories: The Fisherman and the Jinni (Thousand and One Nights)
Sirat Sayf ibn Dhi-Yazan, in which a marid disobeys King Sayf
folklore.beliefs: Marids are part of mainstream Islamic belief about the world of the unseen (al-ghayb); they are not regarded as folklore but as part of the created order.

indigenous.significance: Marids are part of living Islamic religious belief, not a defunct mythology.
indigenous.sensitivity_note: Approach Marids with respect for Islamic theological tradition; distinguish Quranic and theological framing from later Western 'genie' stereotypes.
indigenous.respect_guidelines: Cite Quran, hadith, and recognised tafsir where possible; avoid conflating Marids with Western fantasy 'genies in lamps'.

literature: One Thousand and One Nights (multiple medieval and early modern editions)
Hans Wehr, Dictionary of Modern Written Arabic
games: Marids appear as a class of genie in Dungeons & Dragons (water-aligned genie)
Recurrent in fantasy RPGs drawing on the Arabian Nights
other: Frequently invoked in Western pop-culture treatments of 'genies' and the Arabian Nights

research.ongoing_studies: Marids are studied within Islamic studies, Arabic philology, and the comparative study of jinn and demonology.

sources.title: Alf Layla wa-Layla (One Thousand and One Nights), MacNaghten edition
